needs.statement: Track recurring expenses across all my accounts
needs.label: Track recurring expenses

needs.statement: Catch fraudulent or anomalous charges quickly
needs.label: Catch fraud quickly

needs.statement: Share day-to-day financial state with my partner
needs.label: Share with partner

concepts.name: Weekly auto-digest
concepts.description: A weekly email that automatically categorizes the past week's spending and shows changes from the prior week. No interaction required.

target_needs.hypothesis: Auto-categorization makes recurring spend visible without manual work
Weekly review surfaces anomalies the user might otherwise miss

concepts.past_use_synthesis: Across all participants, the weekly digest was framed as a low-effort way to notice spending creep — small recurring charges that would otherwise be invisible. Three participants explicitly said the appeal was not having to log into anything. P05 was an exception: rated everything positively but with vague, generic language, suggesting halo rather than considered judgment.

past_use_quotes.snippet: I would have loved this last month — I would've seen the Spotify thing immediately.
Auto-categorization is exactly what I want. I'm never going to do it myself.

concepts.name: Manual transaction tagger
concepts.description: Users tag every transaction with a custom category as it comes in. Tags are sharable with a partner who sees the same tagged feed.

target_needs.hypothesis: Manual control yields cleaner, user-defined categories
Shared tags align partners on what counts as what

concepts.past_use_synthesis: Participants split on whether the control was worth the burden. Sharing tags with a partner was the clear win — the only feature in the study that resolves shared-categorization disputes. But three of five participants explicitly said they wouldn't tag transactions themselves, and one described tagging as actively anxiety-inducing.

past_use_quotes.snippet: Same tags, same view, finally a way to align on what counts as 'eating out'.
Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money.
If you stick with the tagging it's the cleanest view possible.

concepts.name: Smart spend alerts
concepts.description: Real-time push notifications when an algorithm detects a transaction that looks unusual relative to your normal spend. User can dismiss, confirm-fraud, or mark-as-expected.

target_needs.hypothesis: Real-time anomaly detection catches fraud at the moment it happens

concepts.past_use_synthesis: C3 was rated by only three of five participants (study ran out of time). Among those three the response was uniformly positive on fraud — the real-time, contextual framing was repeatedly cited as 'exactly what fraud detection should feel like'. P02 rated it `completely` on fraud but verbalized distrust of automated alerts in the same breath, a contradiction worth flagging.

past_use_quotes.snippet: Real-time alerts with context — that's exactly what fraud detection should feel like.

evidence.snippet: I would have loved this last month — I would've seen the Spotify thing immediately.
Auto-categorization is exactly what I want. I'm never going to do it myself.

findings.notes: Strong consensus that auto-categorization is the key driver. P05's `completely` rating is part of a halo pattern (vague generic praise across all needs); does not undermine the verdict but does not strengthen it.

findings.reconciliation_note: Majority `partially` (3/5) with consistent explanations — 'weekly cadence is too slow for fraud'. P05's `completely` is halo; P02's `not_at_all` reinforces the cadence concern. Kept at `partial`.

evidence.snippet: It might catch some stuff but if I see fraud on Monday, this email doesn't help me until Friday.
A weekly email is way too late. Fraud needs to be in seconds, not days.

findings.notes: Cadence is the bottleneck. Concept was designed for fraud detection but the weekly delivery rhythm fundamentally limits effectiveness. Consider real-time fallback for high-value anomalies.

findings.reconciliation_note: P05's `completely` rating is part of a halo pattern (uniform completely across all C1 needs with vague explanations); reduced its weight. 4/5 explicit `not_at_all` with consistent explanations confirms the verdict.

evidence.snippet: This is just for me. My partner would never see it.
Email is one-way. There's no shared aspect to it.

findings.notes: Concept was not targeted at sharing and unanimously confirmed not to address it.

findings.reconciliation_note: Designed-vs-actual gap on adoption likelihood: ratings (2 completely, 3 partially) reflect that participants understand tagging WOULD give the cleanest view, but most explicitly state they wouldn't actually do the tagging. P03's explanation cell is empty — flagged but does not change verdict.

evidence.snippet: If I'm tagging things anyway I'd put 'subscription' on the recurring ones — clearer than auto-categorization.
Theoretically the cleanest. In practice I won't do it.

findings.notes: The disconnect between theoretical and practical addressing is the dominant signal. C2 is designed for N1 but the manual-effort cost makes adoption fragile.

findings.reconciliation_note: Raw majority was `not_at_all` (4/5), which would normally yield `doesn't_address`. P03's explanation explicitly describes the concept as anxiety-inducing — 'tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money'. Even one strong instance of the concept making the user's relationship to the need worse triggers `creates_new_problem` per the verdict rules. Confidence is `low` because the signal is from one participant; surfaced because creates_new_problem is reportable at any confidence.

evidence.snippet: Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money — I'd be anxious about getting it wrong, missing one, mis-tagging it.

findings.notes: Single strong signal — surfaced for further investigation. The risk is that tagging-as-a-mechanism, intended to give control, instead introduces money anxiety. Test in a follow-up study with anxiety-prone users specifically.

evidence.snippet: Same tags, same view, finally a way to align on what counts as 'eating out'.
If my roommate could see the same tags this would solve the entire shared-grocery argument.
We'd both see the same tagged feed — that's the whole solution.

findings.notes: C2 delivers on its target. The shared-tags mechanism resolves an explicit pain (categorization disputes) that participants had concrete past-use stories about.

findings.reconciliation_note: n=3 (sparse) but 2 completely + 1 partially with consistent reasoning that 'an algorithm that knows your normal spend also knows your recurring stuff'. Not targeted, but the addresses verdict holds.

evidence.snippet: If you're catching every weird charge, you're also catching the recurring stuff that drifts.
If it knows your normal spending it knows your subscriptions, so why not.

findings.notes: Good surprise — C3 was designed only for fraud (N2) but the same anomaly-detection mechanism surfaces recurring-charge changes as a side effect.

findings.reconciliation_note: All 3 raters said `completely` with consistent positive reasoning around real-time + contextual content. Confidence is medium rather than high due to small n. P02's contradictory explanation ('I don't really trust automated alerts') is flagged separately but does not undermine the rating.

evidence.snippet: Real-time alerts with context — that's exactly what fraud detection should feel like.
Real-time and contextual — that's exactly the right shape.

findings.notes: C3 delivers on its single targeted need. The contextual alert content (showing what the charge is) was consistently called out as the differentiator from generic bank alerts.

findings.reconciliation_note: Only P01 rated this cell (1× not_at_all). Below the 2-participant threshold for actionable evidence.

evidence.snippet: It's a notification on my phone. My partner doesn't see my phone.

findings.notes: Direction is negative but the cell is structurally under-evidenced. Not actionable.

emergent_needs.label: Splitting recurring shared expenses with roommates
emergent_needs.confidence_note: surfaced in 2 of 5 past-use stories (P02, P04), unprompted; both participants returned to it in spontaneous mentions

evidence.snippet: Honestly the thing I really need is a way to split rent and groceries with my roommates without a shared spreadsheet.
I want something for that — a way to set up shared recurring obligations with people who aren't my partner.

cross_cutting: C1 dominates on tracking recurring expenses but is structurally limited on fraud (cadence) and silent on partner sharing. C2 owns partner sharing but at a real adoption cost — three of five participants explicitly said they wouldn't tag, and one experienced tagging as anxiety-inducing. C3 delivers on fraud and surprisingly also on tracking-via-anomaly, with sparse evidence to confirm. The emergent 'splitting bills with roommates' need is unmet by all three concepts and worth scoping for a future study — partner-sharing as designed assumes a romantic-partner relationship and misses roommate dynamics, which are mentioned by 40% of participants unprompted.
